EO 14009 (signed 2021-01-28, 86 FR 7793-7795), read in full from the held official FR text, states the ACA/Medicaid policy (sec. 1), asks HHS to consider a Special Enrollment Period (sec. 2), orders agency review (sec. 3), revokes EO 13765 and EO 13813 and orders review of related agency actions (sec. 4) and has general provisions (sec. 5). It has no term or sunset; the 'emergency continues' words in sec. 2 are a recital. EO 14148 sec. 2(t) (reading record LSP-EO_14148) revokes it with no effective-date wording, so effective on signing 2025-01-20. The dossier clauses began at sec. 3 and omitted secs. 1 and 2, so the inventory was corrected to ten clauses. Dossier missing lines read: (1) EO 14070 (87 FR 20689, read in full) says it acts 'in addition to' EO 14009 and recites agency actions taken under it; it amends, extends or ends no provision of EO 14009, so it is ruled out as a later event. (2) EO 14177 (read in full) does not name EO 14009. The OFR catalog record for EO 14009 lists 'Supersedes EO 14048', 'EO 14084' and 'See EO 14177', and the record for EO 14177 lists 'EO 14009, September 29, 2023'; those are EO 14109's acts (held EO 14109 sec. 3 supersedes EO 14048 secs. 1-2, sec. 5 amends EO 14084, signed 2023-09-29) printed under a mistyped number, and EO 14109 never names EO 14009, so they are ruled out. Only EO 14148 names EO 14009 as a target among the held texts after 2021. Savings: completed revocations accrue (see savings reason).

Reading record LSP-EO_14148: sec. 2 revokes 78 listed actions, no effective-date wording, so effective on signing 2025-01-20; sec. 3 directs agencies to end implementation and tells the DPC and NEC Directors to review and rescind actions taken under the listed orders; sec. 4(a) is a no-impair clause for statutory authority and OMB functions only; there is no successor delegation, transfer of functions or funds, pending-matter clause or exception for any listed order. Own-residual check, reading EO 14009 in full (secs. 1-5): sec. 4(a) revoked EO 13765 (Minimizing the Economic Burden of the PPACA Pending Repeal) and EO 13813 (Promoting Healthcare Choice and Competition), effective on signing 2021-01-28, a completed act on other orders. EO 14148 sec. 2(t) revokes EO 14009 without revival wording, and revoking a revoking order does not by itself revive the orders it revoked, so those two stay revoked: an effect of EO 14009 survives it (accrued). Secs. 2, 3 and 4(b) only direct HHS and other agency heads to consider or review; any Special Enrollment Period, rule or waiver adopted under them rests on the cited statutes and regulations (42 U.S.C. 18031 and 18041; 45 CFR 155.420(d)(9)) and on EO 14148 sec. 3(b)'s review process, not on a right the order created; sec. 5(c) disclaims private rights. No function, fund or property was transferred. S0 prefill (none_after_bounded_search) OVERRULED to transferred_or_accrued because of the completed revocations. EO 14020 (signed 2021-03-08, 86 FR 13797-13801), read in full from the held official FR text, states the gender-equity policy (sec. 1), establishes the White House Gender Policy Council and its functions, co-chairs and 37-seat membership (sec. 2), requires a government-wide Strategy within 200 days (sec. 3), implementation, reporting and the National Action Plan (sec. 4), terminates the NSPM-16 Working Group (sec. 5), defines terms (sec. 6) and has general provisions (sec. 7). It has no sunset or termination clause for the Council; the dossier's 'sunset_date' lead is the sec. 5 termination of another body and its 'condition' lead is the 'consistent with applicable law' clause, neither an end of this order. EO 14148 sec. 2(bb) revokes the whole order with no effective-date wording, so effective on signing 2025-01-20. The dossier's other actor provision ACT:EO:14020>EO:14168 (sec. 7(b), held FR text 90 FR 8615) rescinds EO 14020 and dissolves the Council on the same day, effective on signing with no delayed wording; it is attached to every clause as a concurrent second end. The dossier inventory stopped inside sec. 3(c) (the segmenter treated the cited 'Executive Order 13985 ...' as a new document, leaving 6,267 characters including all of secs. 4-7 unlisted), so the inventory was corrected by override: the dossier clauses through sec. 3(b) are kept at their spans except three merges of very short clauses (sec. 2(b)(vi)+(vii) and Council seats (g)(i)+(ii) and (g)(iv)+(v), whose quotations the claim-checker cannot verify at under 6 words and 30 characters), and sec. 3(c) and secs. 4-7 are supplied as 16 corrected clauses (75 clauses in all). Dossier missing lines for EO 12250, 13995, 14091, 14121 and 14126 were each read: EO 12250 is cited by EO 14020 sec. 4(a) and predates it; EO 13995 is cited by sec. 3(b); EO 14091, 14121 and 14126 recite or borrow definitions from EO 14020 and amend, extend or end nothing in it. They are ruled out as later events. The Code note at 42 U.S.C. 2000e note (role eo_note_ended_status) states EO 14020 'was revoked by Ex. Ord. No. 14148, sec. 2(bb), Jan. 20, 2025, 90 F.R. 8238, and Ex. Ord. No. 14168, sec. 7(b), Jan. 20, 2025, 90 F.R. 8617', consistent with this ending and the concurrent second end (a machine-extracted lead, not relied on).

Reading record LSP-EO_14148 (official FR text 90 FR 8237, read once in full, text_sha256 65bf2d86... verified on disk): sec. 2 revokes 78 listed executive actions with no effective-date, delayed-effect or phase-in wording, so each revocation took effect on signing, 2025-01-20; sec. 3(b) directs the DPC and NEC Directors to review and rescind, replace or amend agency actions taken under the listed orders (it preserves no provision, office or right of any listed order); sec. 4(a) is a no-impair clause for statutory authority and OMB functions only; there is no successor delegation, no transfer of functions, funds or property, no pending-matter clause and no exception for any listed order. EO 14026 (signed 2021-04-27, 86 FR 22835-22838), read in full from the held FR text, raises the minimum wage for covered federal contractors to $15.00 from 2022-01-30 and then by Secretary of Labor determination (sec. 2), sets the tipped-worker wage (sec. 3), directs DOL regulations by 2021-11-24 and FAR amendments (sec. 4), gives DOL enforcement authority (sec. 5), revokes EO 13838 and supersedes EO 13658 'as of January 30, 2022' (sec. 6), and sets applicability and effective-date rules (secs. 8-9). The machine own-term kinds are 'condition' (the appropriations and 'to the extent permitted by law' conditions), 'fixed_term' (the 60-day periods in secs. 4(a), 4(b) and the sec. 9(b) 60-day solicitation window) and none of them is an end; the order has no sunset or termination clause, and the dated figures ($15.00 from 2022-01-30 and so on) are wage start dates. EO 14236 (signed 2025-03-14, 90 FR 13037-13038, held FR text, read in full; reading record LSP-EO_14236) sec. 2(d) revokes EO 14026 by name with no effective-date wording, so the revocation took effect on signing. A by-number scan (whitespace and hyphenation normalised) of all 6,652 held FR-original texts finds EO 14026 named only in EO 14236, so no amendment before the end is held and no other order extends or reinstates it. Savings: see savings_residuals (continuing_independent, from the implementing regulations and contract clauses that survive the revocation of the order). Inventory: the dossier's 32 clauses cover secs. 1-10 from the Policy section through sec. 10(c), no gap or overlap; no correction needed. Several clauses cross a page break and so contain the running head of the next page, as the dossier segmented them.

Reading record LSP-EO_14236 (EO 14236, 90 FR 13037-13038, read once in full): sec. 2 revokes eighteen executive actions by name, EO 14026 in sec. 2(d); sec. 3 is a general non-impairment, implementation and no-rights clause; there is no savings, pending-matter, transition or rescission-direction provision for any revoked action. EO 14049 (signed 2021-10-11, 86 FR 57313-57318), read in full from the held official FR text, establishes the White House Initiative in the Department of Education (sec. 2), makes the National Advisory Council on Indian Education its advisory council (sec. 3), sets administrative provisions and revokes EO 13592 (sec. 4), defines terms (sec. 5) and has general provisions (sec. 6). It has no term or sunset: the only timing words are the 180-day deadline for Memoranda of Agreement (sec. 2(d)) and the annual report 'no later than 1 year after the date of this order and annually thereafter' (sec. 2(i)); neither is an end, and no clause needs a report date to find its end. EO 14055 (signed 2021-11-18, 86 FR 66397-66401), read in full from the held official FR text: sec. 1 policy; sec. 2 definitions; sec. 3 nondisplacement contract clause; sec. 4 location continuity; sec. 5 exclusions; sec. 6 agency exceptions; sec. 7 Labor regulations, FAR amendment and OMB guidance; sec. 8 enforcement; sec. 9 revokes EO 13897; sec. 10 severability; sec. 11 effective date (effective immediately, applying to solicitations after the FAR Council's action: an applicability rule, not an end); sec. 12 general provisions. The order has no term or sunset; the 180-day and 60-day deadlines (sec. 7) are deadlines for action and the 'up to 3 years' debarment (sec. 8(a)) is a sanction length. EO 14148 sec. 2(qq) (held text 90 FR 8237-8241, item at char 8176; reading record LSP-EO_14148) revokes EO 14055 by number; EO 14148 has no effective-date wording anywhere, so the revocation took effect on signing, January 20, 2025 (2025-01-28 is only the FR printing date). Every clause's first end is therefore 2025-01-20. Inventory: the dossier's 31 clauses cover sec. 1 to sec. 12(c); the 20-character sec. 2 heading is merged into sec. 2(a) by an inventory override (30 clauses, exact spans); the enacting clause, page furniture and signature block are not operative. D6: no held official text other than EO 14148 names EO 14055 (EO 14236 is held and does not name it) and the OFR catalog records only EO 14148, so no later event changed any clause before the end. Savings: continuing_independent (29 CFR part 9 and awarded contract clauses, leads only).

Reading record LSP-EO_14148 (instruments/01/readings, text_sha256 65bf2d86... re-verified against the held text): sec. 2 revokes 78 listed actions, EO 14055 at sec. 2(qq), with no effective-date wording (effective on signing 2025-01-20); sec. 3(a) tells agencies to end implementation and sec. 3(b) tells the DPC and NEC Directors to review and rescind, replace or amend actions taken under the listed orders; sec. 4(a) is a no-impair clause for statutory authority and OMB functions only; there is no savings, pending-matter, transfer or exception wording for any listed order, and no revival wording. Own-residual check, reading EO 14055 in full (secs. 1-12): the order created no body and disclaims private rights (sec. 12(c); sec. 8(b) creates no Contract Disputes Act rights), but it directed the Secretary of Labor to issue implementing regulations and the FAR Council to amend the FAR (sec. 7), and required a nondisplacement clause in covered solicitations and contracts (sec. 3). The dossier's current-law leads show the Department of Labor rule at 29 CFR part 9 (secs. 9.1, 9.4, 9.5, 9.11, 9.12, 9.23, Appendix A contract clause) still in the eCFR as of 2026-10-14, and contract clauses already awarded stay contract terms until modified. EO 14148 says nothing about that rule or those clauses, so they continue independently of the revoked order until the Department of Labor, the FAR Council or the parties change them. EO 14089 (signed 2022-12-13, 87 FR 77459-77461), read in full from the held official FR text, states the policy (sec. 1), directs the Secretary of State to establish the President's Advisory Council on African Diaspora Engagement within 180 days (sec. 2), fixes membership, 2-year member terms, a Chair and Executive Director (sec. 3), functions (sec. 4), administration with quarterly meetings (sec. 5) and general provisions including FACA (sec. 6). It has no termination or sunset clause. EO 14148 sec. 2(aaa) (reading record LSP-EO_14148) revokes it with no effective-date wording, effective on signing 2025-01-20. Dossier missing lines read: (1) EO 14109 (88 FR 68447, read in full; effective 2023-09-29 under its sec. 6) sec. 1(cc) continues the Council until 2025-09-30; it is attached as a later event to the Council clauses (secs. 2 through 6(a)); it extends the committee's FACA life, amends no text, and the continuance date falls after the 2025-01-20 revocation, so it does not move the first end. (2) EO 13985 (held official text) does not name EO 14089; EO 14089 sec. 4(b)(i) only refers to the efforts coordinated under EO 13985, and EO 13985 was revoked by EO 14148 sec. 2(a) on the same day, so it changes nothing earlier and is ruled out. The 2-year member terms are not an end of the clauses. The inventory is the dossier's 22 contiguous clauses from sec. 1 to the signature line and is kept. No other held official text names EO 14089. Savings: none found.

Reading record LSP-EO_14148: sec. 2 revokes 78 listed actions, no effective-date wording, so effective on signing 2025-01-20; sec. 3 directs agencies to end implementation and tells the DPC and NEC Directors to review and rescind actions taken under the listed orders; sec. 4(a) is a no-impair clause for statutory authority and OMB functions only; there is no successor delegation, transfer of functions or funds, pending-matter clause or exception for any listed order. Own-residual check, reading EO 14089 in full (secs. 1-6): it revokes or amends no order, transfers no function, fund or property and creates no right (sec. 6(d)). It created an advisory council in the Department of State whose appointments are made by the Secretary of State for 2-year terms without compensation; the Council, its terms and its advice function ended with the order. The one residual lead is EO 14109 sec. 1(cc), which continued the Council as a FACA committee until 2025-09-30 and was not itself revoked by EO 14148; that continuance only extends a committee that Executive Order 14089 established and supplies no separate mandate, appointment power or duty, and EO 14148 is the later and specific act ending the order, so no continuing effect is found. Section 3(b) of Executive Order 14148 directs the Director of the Domestic Policy Council and the Director of the National Economic Council to review all Federal Government actions taken pursuant to the orders, memoranda and proclamations listed in section 2 and to take necessary steps to rescind, replace or amend such actions as appropriate. Because rescission of actions already taken is left to later action, Federal actions already taken under Executive Order 14096 before 2025-01-20 were not themselves revoked by section 2 and stood until rescinded, replaced or amended individually. No held source identifies a particular surviving action or its later fate, so none is asserted. The earlier instruments revoked or amended by the clauses executed on the order's own date stay revoked or amended: those acts are accrued effects not undone by section 2 of Executive Order 14148, and Executive Order 12898 is not listed in section 2 of Executive Order 14148, so text inserted into it by section 7 was not revoked by that order. Section 3(a)(i) of Executive Order 14173 of 2025-01-21 (Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity) later revokes Executive Order 12898 itself; that revocation acts on Executive Order 12898, not on any clause of this order, so it is not a later event or end for this order.

Section 4(a) of Executive Order 14154 of 2025-01-20 (90 FR 8353) lists this order among executive orders that are revoked and states that any offices established in them are abolished. EO 14115 (signed 2024-02-01, 89 FR 7605-7608), read in full from the held official FR text, finds a threat to the peace, security and stability of the West Bank and declares a national emergency, blocks the property of persons determined under sec. 1 (secs. 1-3), suspends their entry (sec. 4), prohibits evasion and conspiracy (sec. 5), makes IEEPA determinations on donations and notice (secs. 6 and 8), defines terms (sec. 7), authorizes Treasury rules and redelegation (sec. 9), excepts official business (sec. 10), provides for reports to the Congress (sec. 11) and has general provisions (sec. 12). The order has no term, sunset or termination clause: its only dossier own-term leads are the 'consistent with applicable law' condition and the sec. 4(d) comparison to Proclamation 8693, neither an end. EO 14148 sec. 2(hhh) revokes the whole order with no effective-date wording, so effective on signing 2025-01-20. The dossier has no missing line, conflict or current-law lead for this order. The dossier inventory (43 clauses) began after the findings paragraph and split sec. 1(b)(ii) in the middle of a sentence, so the inventory was corrected by override: the preamble findings are added as one clause, and the two fragments of sec. 1(b)(ii) are merged, and the two short items of sec. 1(a)(i)(B), (3) and (4), are merged (too short for the claim-checker to verify) (42 clauses in all). The national-emergency question is stated in the lead clause and in savings_residuals. No amendment, extension, partial revocation or supersession of EO 14115 appears in any held text or OFR edge before 2025-01-20. The Code note at 50 U.S.C. 1701 note ('West Bank') states 'Ex. Ord. No. 14115, Feb. 1, 2024, 89 F.R. 7605, revoked by Ex. Ord. No. 14148, sec. 2(hhh), Jan. 20, 2025, 90 F.R. 8240', consistent with this ending (a machine-extracted lead, not relied on).

Reading record LSP-EO_14148 (official FR text 90 FR 8237, read once in full, text_sha256 65bf2d86... verified on disk): sec. 2 revokes 78 listed executive actions with no effective-date, delayed-effect or phase-in wording, so each revocation took effect on signing, 2025-01-20; sec. 3(b) directs the DPC and NEC Directors to review and rescind, replace or amend agency actions taken under the listed orders (it preserves no provision, office or right of any listed order); sec. 4(a) is a no-impair clause for statutory authority and OMB functions only; there is no successor delegation, no transfer of functions, funds or property, no pending-matter clause and no exception for any listed order. Own-residual check, reading EO 14115 in full (preamble and secs. 1-12): the order declared a national emergency under IEEPA and the NEA, blocked all property and interests in property of persons determined under sec. 1 and suspended their entry (sec. 4), and sec. 9 authorized the Treasury Secretary to issue rules and to redelegate functions within Treasury. Effects of the order that attached before 2025-01-20 are not undone by its revocation: property blocked and transactions prohibited or evaded under secs. 1-5 before that date, and any liability for violations before it, are accrued matters of an IEEPA instrument, and EO 14148 sec. 2(hhh) revokes the order with no savings clause and no statement of what happens to them (accrued). The sec. 9 redelegation authority and any Treasury listings made under it are exercises of functions the order conferred; they end with the order and no redelegation or regulation under it appears in the eCFR machine search. The national emergency declared in the preamble is not terminated by EO 14148 in so many words; if it was not continued by a notice published within 90 days before 2025-02-01 it lapsed under 50 U.S.C. 1622(d) after the first end, and I found no such notice in any held source, so the claim relies on the revocation of the order as the first end and asserts nothing about the emergency after it. Prefill was 'review' (S1_transfer_wording): decided from the reading and the order as transferred_or_accrued. Bounded search: every held official FR text (EO 1 through EO 14435) was searched for the number 14115 and the title; only EO 14148 sec. 2(hhh) names it as a target (the EO 9372 and 9386 hits are page-index numbers); OFR edges list only EO 14148 and the Proclamation 8693 cross-reference; the three machine searches were read.

Executive Order 6206-A (July 16, 1933) is a final approval, with amendments set out in Schedule A, of the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Textile Industry under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act. Read in full from the held American Presidency Project transcription (page record checked; identity, date and subject confirmed against the census register and the WPA 1944 list); the withdrawal of the termination condition leaves the approval without a four-month end. Its command depends entirely on the code approval, so its first end is the repeal of the code-approval and code-enforcement provisions of Title I by section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 on June 14, 1935, applying SHARED_ANALYSIS.md and its adjudication; Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization only.

Paragraph 5 of Schedule A begins \"Until adoption of further provisions of this Code that may prove necessary\", which is a term of the code that depends on later code provisions and not a limit on the approval, and paragraph 1 asks a code agency to report \"prior to January 1, 1934\", which is a deadline and not an end. Held later orders naming the Cotton Textile Code are: EO 6242-C, 6242-D and 6242-E (denials of company applications for exemption, each excepting the Administrator's stay of July 30, 1933 on the machine-hour provision as applied to tire yarns); EO 6407 and EO 6476 (denial of that exemption and termination of the stay, effective November 13 and December 11, 1933); EO 6424 and EO 6463 (extensions of the stay's termination date); EO 6420-A (approval of modifications \"made a part of said code\"); EO 6858 (September 26, 1934: creates the Textile Labor Relations Board and, in section 9, abolishes the Cotton Textile National Industrial Relations Board created by section XVII of the code as amended July 10, 1934); and EO 6876 (approval of an amendment). Acts done and liabilities incurred under the approved code before June 14, 1935 are accrued consequences, and the section 5 exemption from the antitrust laws for action complying with an approved code taken while Title I was in effect is likewise an accrued effect for completed action. The proviso to section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 names agreements and action under them, not codes, and states no time limit; the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the section 5 exemption for past action under codes, and whatever exemption survives for past action is an accrued effect, not continued operation of this approval. Nothing in the held sources continues the approval after June 14, 1935.

Schechter, 295 U.S. 495, held the code provisions in question invalid on both of its grounds; recorded as a validity characterization of section 3 code approvals, not as an end date for this order. It adjudicated the Live Poultry Code provisions and cancelled or withdrew no other approving order.

Sections 3(a)-(f) state the legal effects of an approved code that section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed: the code's provisions became the standards of fair competition (3(b)), district courts could restrain violations (3(c)), and violations were misdemeanors (3(f)).

This order is a presidential approval, under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, of the Code of Fair Competition for the Farm Equipment Industry: "do order that the said code of fair competition be and is hereby approved, except that the second paragraph of article VIII must be eliminated". Its only legal effect depended on that code (NIRA section 3(b) made the code's provisions the standards of fair competition). Congress approved S.J. Res. 113 on June 14, 1935, and section 2 repealed the provisions of Title I that delegated power to approve or prescribe codes and provided for their enforcement, so the approval had no operative effect after that date. Schechter's May 27, 1935 holding that the section 3 delegation was unconstitutional is recorded as a validity characterization and not as an end date, following the reviewed shared analysis. The text relied on is the American Presidency Project transcription, so the original is not yet held and the quotation must be re-checked when an official copy is retrieved.

An approval of a code under section 3 of title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act had legal effect only through section 3: under 3(b) the code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade or industry and a violation in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce was an unfair method of competition under the Federal Trade Commission Act, under 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations and district attorneys were directed to sue, and under 3(f) each violation was a misdemeanor (the section 3 excerpt held in this packet). Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935 (49 Stat. 375), repealed 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes' and states no effective date other than its approval. United States, 295 U.S. 495 (decided May 27, 1935), held the section 3 code-making delegation unconstitutional ('we hold the code provisions here in question to be invalid'); the held excerpts record that as a validity characterization (an approval under an unconstitutional delegation was void from issuance under the doctrine then prevailing, and May 27, 1935 is when that was declared), not as an end date, because the judgment cancelled no other approving order and a later doctrine treats a measure's earlier existence as an operative fact. An approval of a code under section 3 of title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act had legal effect only through section 3: under 3(b) the code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade or industry and a violation in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce was an unfair method of competition under the Federal Trade Commission Act, under 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations and district attorneys were directed to sue, and under 3(f) each violation was a misdemeanor (the section 3 excerpt held in this packet). Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935 (49 Stat. 375), repealed 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes' and states no effective date other than its approval. That repeal removed the power the approval rested on and every provision through which the approved code was enforced, which is the reason (not a default date) that it ends the prospective operative effect of this command on June 14, 1935. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U.S. 495 (decided May 27, 1935), held the section 3 code-making delegation unconstitutional ('we hold the code provisions here in question to be invalid'); the held excerpts record that as a validity characterization (an approval under an unconstitutional delegation was void from issuance under the doctrine then prevailing, and May 27, 1935 is when that was declared), not as an end date, because the judgment cancelled no other approving order and a later doctrine treats a measure's earlier existence as an operative fact. June 16, 1935 is not an end: section 1 of the resolution replaced the two-year expiry in section 2(c) with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2.

EO 6663 (March 31, 1934), read in full in the held American Presidency Project transcription (two held copies of the same page, sha256 shared), exempts Luther L. Browning, linotype machinist in charge, Government Printing Office from section 204 of the Economy Act of June 30, 1932 and continues the employee in the service until April 1, 1935. Identity: number, date, person and title agree across the APP page, the census register and the WPA 1944 numbered list. Later orders further exempting the same person are held and added to this packet as source-supplement excerpts: EO 6984 (March 7, 1935) recites EO 6663 and further exempts Browning until April 1, 1936; EO 7307 (February 28, 1936) recites EO 6663 and EO 6984 and further exempts him until November 1, 1936. Each is recorded as a later event on the clause (clauses.csv). Extension reading, decided on the texts: each later order is a new exercise of the section 204 proviso with its own period. None says that the earlier order 'is amended' or alters its date; each recites the earlier exemption as a past grant ('who was exempted ... by Executive Order No. ...') and grants a further exemption 'until' a new date. The held extension texts confirm the reading: EO 6984 recites Browning as 'exempted from compulsory retirement for a period of 1 year by Executive Order No. 6663', and EO 7307 recites him as exempted 'for a period of two years by Executive Orders No. 6663 ... and No. 6984', counting each earlier order as a completed period. The strike-and-insert ruling does not apply because nothing is struck or inserted. So this order's own command ended on its own stated date, inclusive (exclusive alternative: ended when that day began), and each extension is recorded as a later event naming the same employee; the employee's exempt status continued without a gap under the extension orders. The alternative reading, that the extensions prolonged this order's command, would put its first end at the last extension's 'until' date (1936-11-01, inclusive); the texts do not support it, because no extension operates on this order's text. Legal reading: ends by its own terms on 1935-04-01, inclusive. The census, WPA and full-text name searches found no further order naming this person after the last extension. Authority: section 204 of Part II of the Legislative Appropriation Act of June 30, 1932 (47 Stat. 382, 404), whose proviso lets the President exempt a person from automatic separation at retirement age. No held source shows section 204 repealed or amended before this order's stated end. Held texts of later exemptions show the President still granting exemptions under section 204 after this date (for example EO 7725 of October 1937, under section 204, running to November 1, 1938), which corroborates that the statutory scheme ran through the stated date.

EO 6678 was read in full in the registered APP transcription (common-crawl capture 2025-12-14T13:52:27Z). Identity: the census register row, the WPA 1944 numbered list (1934 Apr 14, p. 574, 'Provisions to meet the expenses incurred in the administration of any code of fair competition by the various code authorities, prescribed') and the APP page record with the same sha256 agree on number, date and subject; the page heading names the order's number, its date matches, and the page record's text_sha256 equals the held file's. The order prescribes, under Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act and 'in order to effectuate the purposes of said Title', a clause on collecting the expenses of code administration. It orders that the clause or an appropriate modification 'shall become effective as a part of any code of fair competition approved under said Title', on application under the code's amendment provisions or by representative trade associations, if the Administrator finds the clause necessary to effectuate the policy of Title I. Section 1 of the clause authorizes the Code Authority, subject to the Administrator's approval, to incur obligations, to submit a budget and a basis of contribution, and to secure contributions, including by suit in its own name; section 2 limits participation in selecting the Code Authority and use of the NRA emblem to members that comply with the code and contribute. It is a general rule for all approved codes rather than the approval of one named code, so the shared analysis does not decide it directly; it is treated here as a code-dependent standing prescription because every command in it takes effect only as part of an approved code. Under the shared reviewed analysis (SHARED_ANALYSIS.md, ADJUDICATION.json) a code-dependent command that did not end earlier ended on June 14, 1935, when section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed the power to approve or prescribe codes and the provisions enforcing them; Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded only as a validity characterization. Original not yet held; the working text is a labeled transcription under the 2026-10-21 owner ruling.

Executive Order 6684-C (April 19, 1934) is an approval of the Electrical Contracting Chapter of the Code of Fair Competition for the Construction Industry, and a modification of the earlier approval of that code to cover the code as supplemented, under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act. Read in full from the held American Presidency Project transcription (APP node 362453), registered as grade mirror_transcription (not an original). Identity and page check: the page record is a Common Crawl capture of 2025-12-08T01:28:26Z whose heading names Executive Order 6684-C, whose date (April 19, 1934) and subject agree with the text, and whose text sha256 equals the held text's. The census register and the WPA 1944 list (1934 Apr 19, p.575, approval of the code for the Electrical Contracting Division of the Construction Industry) give the same date and subject. The order's own text states no limit on the approval. Its command depends entirely on the code approval, so its first end is the repeal of the code-approval and code-enforcement provisions of Title I by section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 on June 14, 1935, applying SHARED_ANALYSIS.md and its adjudication; Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization only.

Acts done and liabilities incurred under the approved code before June 14, 1935 are accrued consequences, and the section 5 exemption from the antitrust laws for action complying with an approved code taken while Title I was in effect is likewise an accrued effect for completed action. The proviso to section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 names agreements and action under them, not codes, and states no time limit; the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the section 5 exemption for past action under codes, and whatever exemption survives for past action is an accrued effect, not continued operation of this approval. Nothing in the held sources continues the approval after June 14, 1935.

A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U.S. 495, decided May 27, 1935: the Court held the section 3 code-making delegation unconstitutional and the Live Poultry Code provisions in question invalid. Recorded as a validity characterization for every section 3 code approval, not as this order's end; the judgment did not cancel or withdraw this order.

NIRA section 3 (48 Stat. 195, June 16, 1933): under 3(a) the President approved codes and could impose conditions of approval; under 3(b), 3(c) and 3(f) an approved code's provisions became standards of fair competition enforceable by injunction and as misdemeanors. These are the legal effects that section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed.

NIRA section 5 exempted from the antitrust laws any code approved and in effect under Title I and any complying action while Title I was in effect and for sixty days thereafter; any exemption for action taken before the repeal is an accrued effect, not continued operation of the approval.

EO 6684-D (1934-04-19, Franklin D. Roosevelt), read in full in the held American Presidency Project transcription (registered grade mirror_transcription, not an original; 2478 characters). Identity: the census register lists it as 'Executive Order 6684-D—Code of Fair Competition for the Household Goods Storage & Moving Trade' dated 1934-04-19; the WPA 1944 list has '1934 Apr 19 p.575: Code of Fair Competition for the Household Goods Storage and Moving Trade conditionallyapproved. IX NRA Codes 349.'. Page check: the mirror page record with the same source sha256 is headed 'Executive Order 6684-D—Code of Fair Competition for the Household Goods Storage & Moving Trade', dated 1934-04-19, from a common-crawl capture of 2025-09-11T05:23:22Z, and its text_sha256 equals the held text's; the heading names this order's number and the date and subject agree with the text. Machine inventory corrected: it is one paragraph (742-2442) holding four distinct commands, split below. (1) The approval: "do order that the said Code of Fair Competition be and it is hereby approved", the Code of Fair Competition for the Household Goods Storage & Moving Trade (title I, section 3(a)). (2) A stay of the waiting period in Article VII, Section 1 "pending further order by the Administrator either within a period of sixty (60) days from the effective date of this Code or after the completion of a study of open price associations". (3) An understanding about the question for the public hearing to be held before June 15, 1934. (4) A stay of Article II, Section 1(c) "pending the public hearing to be held prior to June 15, 1934, and pending my further order". None states a fixed end date: the sixty-day phrase and the hearing date are times by which the Administrator or the President was to act, and every stay waits on a further order, so none has an own-terms end before June 14, 1935. First end of every clause: S.J. Res. 113 section 2, June 14, 1935; no earlier end is held.

EO 6684-E (signed April 19, 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt) approves the Mason Contractors Chapter of the Code of Fair Competition for the Construction Industry (approved January 31, 1934) and modifies the previous approval of that code so that it covers the code as supplemented by the chapter. Both commands are section 3 approval commands in one sentence, and both depend on the code-approval provisions of Title I. Identity: the census register row, the WPA 1944 numbered list entry at p. 575 and the held text agree on number, date and subject. Source: the American Presidency Project transcription (a Common Crawl capture, grade mirror_transcription, acceptable_as_original false); the page record with the same sha256 names this order's number, its date and subject agree with the text, and its text_sha256 is the held text's. The claim follows the reviewed shared analysis of NIRA code approvals: first end June 14, 1935 by statutory repeal (S.J. Res. 113 section 2); Schechter recorded as a validity characterization, not an end date; accrued effects survive as past effects.

Schechter, 295 U.S. 495, held the code provisions in question invalid on the delegation ground and on the intrastate-commerce ground. It is recorded as a validity characterization of every section 3 code approval (void from issuance under the doctrine prevailing in 1935), not as an end of this order; the judgment did not cancel or withdraw this approval.

Section 3 of Title I states the legal effects of an approved code that section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed by description: under 3(b) its provisions are the standards of fair competition for the trade or industry, under 3(c) the district courts may restrain violations, and under 3(f) a violation is a misdemeanor. Cited for the content of the repealed provisions, not for any date.

Executive Order 6685 of April 20, 1934 approves amendments to the Code of Fair Competition for the Distilled Spirits Rectifying Industry and modifies the December 9, 1933 order approving that code, under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act (NIRA); its only operative command is that amendment and modification. The text states no period, condition, 'until' date or provisional approval, and no held record cancels, suspends, supersedes or modifies the approval under section 10(b) before June 14, 1935. The approval had legal effect only through section 3 (standards of fair competition under 3(b), equity enforcement under 3(c), misdemeanor liability under 3(f)). Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 (49 Stat. 375), approved June 14, 1935, repealed the provisions delegating power to approve or prescribe codes and providing for their enforcement, so the best supported first end of the approval's prospective operative effect is June 14, 1935. Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization, not an end date, and June 16, 1935 is not an end. Acts and liabilities before the repeal are accrued effects.

June 14, 1935 is the supported repeal event for code approval/prescription/enforcement powers, not a proven universal first cessation. Schechter's section 3 delegation holding cannot be dismissed because this particular order was not cancelled by name. The October 21 unnamed-instrument constraint and October 28 evidence rule remain unreconciled with any categorical first-end shortcut. June 16, 1935 was replaced as the scheduled Title I expiry; April 1, 1936 is a conditional outer statutory limit, not this member's demonstrated first end. The study is due three months after the CODE effective date, not three months after this order's April 20 signature. Neither that starting date nor actual submission is established. No report deadline supplies cessation.

The original numbers 1–5 are findings, not operative duties. Paragraph 6 directs the Code Authority to submit a labor-conditions study; the final paragraph approves the code. The native six-item inventory omits a separately bounded final approval and treats findings as clauses; retain the old producer's two-command correction as a useful inventory lead, subject to exact revalidation.

The Code Authority must submit to the Administrator a study of hours, pay and working conditions with a view to revision. Section 3(a) supports treating it as an approval condition, but its past-operations study content requires examination against the retained administrative functions in 7075/7076. Neither the actor label nor the repeal alone proves that a past-due report ceased being required.

Distinguish completed performance and surviving records/institutions from prospective code enforcement. NIRA section 5 and S.J. Res. 113's proviso do not establish universal surviving liabilities, universal agreement conversion, or continuation of every administrative direction. No general savings-law source has been established in this application. The status and scope of any accrued rights/liabilities remain qualified.

shared_rationale_references.resolved_text: Route the exact old three-clause June 14 claim; committee designation, recommendations and reporting are distinct unresolved acts.

June 14, 1935 is the supported repeal event for code approval/prescription/enforcement powers, not a proven universal first cessation. Schechter's section 3 delegation holding cannot be dismissed because this particular order was not cancelled by name. The October 21 unnamed-instrument constraint and October 28 evidence rule remain unreconciled with any categorical first-end shortcut. June 16, 1935 was replaced as the scheduled Title I expiry; April 1, 1936 is a conditional outer statutory limit, not this member's demonstrated first end. Ninety days is a recommendation deadline with no explicit starting point in this text; December 1, 1934 is the operation-report deadline. Neither proves submission or cancellation.

The operative lead approves the code subject to conditions. Item (1) combines industry designation, Administrator approval of membership, cooperation on standards and recommendations. Item (a) separately requires an industry report. Recitals of prior Administrator reporting do not prove these future acts. The old item (a) span includes signature/recommendation boilerplate; bound the operative report text separately on replacement.

The industry must designate the committee, whose membership needs approval; it then cooperates on quality/labelling standards for code inclusion. The industry report reviews hours/wages in Articles III/IV. These are section 3 approval conditions but contain actual acts and a study of past operation. Post-repeal continuation of compatible administrative work defeats automatic extinction by label without proving these duties continued.

Distinguish completed performance and surviving records/institutions from prospective code enforcement. NIRA section 5 and S.J. Res. 113's proviso do not establish universal surviving liabilities, universal agreement conversion, or continuation of every administrative direction. No general savings-law source has been established in this application. The status and scope of any accrued rights/liabilities remain qualified.

Legal basis for the first end. An approval of a code under section 3 of title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act had legal effect only through section 3: under 3(b) the code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade or industry and a violation in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce was an unfair method of competition under the Federal Trade Commission Act, under 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations and district attorneys were directed to sue, and under 3(f) each violation was a misdemeanor (the section 3 excerpt held in this packet). Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935 (49 Stat. 375), repealed 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes' and states no effective date other than its approval. That repeal removed the power the approval rested on and every provision through which the approved code was enforced, which is the reason (not a default date) that it ends the prospective operative effect of this command on June 14, 1935. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U.S. 495 (decided May 27, 1935), held the section 3 code-making delegation unconstitutional ('we hold the code provisions here in question to be invalid'); the held excerpts record that as a validity characterization (an approval under an unconstitutional delegation was void from issuance under the doctrine then prevailing, and May 27, 1935 is when that was declared), not as an end date, because the judgment cancelled no other approving order and a later doctrine treats a measure's earlier existence as an operative fact. June 16, 1935 is not an end: section 1 of the resolution replaced the two-year expiry in section 2(c) with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2.

EO 6861 (September 28, 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt), made 'in order to effectuate the purposes of said title', orders: (1) that the amendments to Articles III and IV of the Cotton Garment Code approved by EO 6828 'be stayed up to and including October 15, 1934'; (2) that the National Industrial Recovery Board 'shall forthwith appoint a committee of three impartial persons' who will 'hear said protests, investigate the facts and report its recommendations on or before October 10, 1934'; (3) that the Board 'shall immediately transmit said recommendations to me'. This is a mixed order, so each command has its own end. The machine inventory (a lead plus three items) is corrected to the three commands. Clause 1 (the stay): EO 6871 (October 12, 1934), paragraph 1, orders 'That paragraph numbered 1 of Executive Order No. 6861 ... be and it is hereby revoked.' The first end is that revocation on 1934-10-12, three days before the stay's own stated end (October 15, inclusive; exclusive reading: when October 15 began). EO 6871 paragraph 2 stays the same amendments to and including December 1, 1934; that is a separate new stay by the later order, recorded as a later event, not an extension of this stay (the stay and the revocation are express, so the strike-and-insert and further-exemption rulings do not turn the revocation into an amendment). Clause 2 (committee): EO 6871 recites that the Board 'pursuant to said Executive Order duly appointed Willard E. Hotchkiss, W. Jett Lauck and Donald M. Nelson ... as such committee, which said committee thereafter heard protests, investigated the facts and on October 10, 1934, did report its recommendations'. The command (appoint, hear, report by October 10) was performed and is exhausted on 1934-10-10, the date of the report; the appointment fell between September 28 and October 10. EO 6871 paragraph 3 continues the committee with new instructions on its own authority, which is a later event of the committee, not a continuation of this command. Clause 3 (transmittal): EO 6871 states that the President 'do[es] hereby approve and adopt the report and recommendations of said committee' on October 12, 1934, so the recommendations had reached him by then; the report was made on October 10. The transmittal was therefore made between October 10 and October 12, 1934. The exact day is not stated; the clause is dated 1934-10-12, the day by which the evidence shows performance, and the interval is stated. The order does not state that the Board itself carried the document, only that the recommendations had reached the President; that is the object of the command.

EO6871 paragraph 1 expressly revokes the stay October 12, before its inclusive October 15 own-term endpoint. Its new December 1 stay is a later distinct command. No demand for an exact appointment date should erase the observed appointment interval.

The report and committee are surviving results of completed acts; EO6871 continues the committee with further work and establishes a new stay. Nothing warrants treating report delivery as committee dissolution. The old report mission can be functionally completed while the same institution survives.

shared_rationale_references.resolved_text: Route the exact old June 14 amendment/appointment claim; the revised commission condition continues in the parent order and actual appointments are unresolved.

June 14, 1935 is the supported repeal event for code approval/prescription/enforcement powers, not a proven universal first cessation. Schechter's section 3 delegation holding cannot be dismissed because this particular order was not cancelled by name. The October 21 unnamed-instrument constraint and October 28 evidence rule remain unreconciled with any categorical first-end shortcut. June 16, 1935 was replaced as the scheduled Title I expiry; April 1, 1936 is a conditional outer statutory limit, not this member's demonstrated first end. The strike-and-insert ruling calls for an amendment later event and parent continuity, not a first end on October 11. Original 10-day appointment term does not carry into the replacement merely by habit; this text recites failed nominee agreement, not completed appointments.

The operative revision changes the quoted first portion of condition 4 of EO6756B. Before: three members appointed by Administrator within ten days after the effective date, with three nomination sources. After: four members appointed by Board; Puerto Rico representative one vote, two mainland representatives one-half vote each, impartial chairman one vote. The replaced text removes the ten-day phrase. The parent condition's study and recommendation sentences are not quoted as replaced and remain relevant. Parent condition 5 also assigns a 90-day recommendation role to the Needlework Commission alongside the Piece Rates Commission. Also retain the present approval of the National Industrial Recovery Board report in the recital (the report is said to be attached). The attachment is absent from the held representation; full operative inventory cannot be certified until its scope and any incorporated recommendations are checked.

Board appointment and institutional composition are future commands. The parent mandates studying relative operation in Puerto Rico and mainland industries and permits recommendations; this is broader than mere prospective compliance. The old claim's premise that a commission studying a code necessarily disappears with code enforcement requires evidence, especially under 7075/7076.

Distinguish completed performance and surviving records/institutions from prospective code enforcement. NIRA section 5 and S.J. Res. 113's proviso do not establish universal surviving liabilities, universal agreement conversion, or continuation of every administrative direction. No general savings-law source has been established in this application. The status and scope of any accrued rights/liabilities remain qualified.

Decision on its own terms. The order's one command is the rewrite of paragraph 6; under the strike-and-insert ruling the rewritten paragraph is the operative clause and continues, amended, until something ends it. Two candidate ends exist in held evidence. (a) The inserted text's own period: the paragraph excepts positions only 'from this date to February 1, 1935'. Under the evidence-decides ruling EO 7209 is not a default end, and here the earlier own-terms end is evidenced. Savings: appointments made under the exception during its period are accrued; they do not keep the exception operative. Executive Order 6945 (January 10, 1935) is an approval of an amendment to the Code of Fair Competition for the Distilled Spirits Rectifying Industry and a modification of the earlier approval to cover the code as amended, under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act. Read in full from the held American Presidency Project transcription. Identity, date and subject agree with the census register and the WPA 1944 list (page 600, January 10, 1935). Res. 113 on June 14, 1935, applying SHARED_ANALYSIS.md and its adjudication; Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization only.

Read in full from the held American Presidency Project transcription, registered as grade mirror_transcription (not an original). Its command depends entirely on the code approval, so its first end is the repeal of the code-approval and code-enforcement provisions of Title I by section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 on June 14, 1935, applying SHARED_ANALYSIS.md and its adjudication; Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization only.

Acts done and liabilities incurred under the approved code before June 14, 1935 are accrued consequences, and the section 5 exemption from the antitrust laws for action complying with an approved code taken while Title I was in effect is likewise an accrued effect for completed action. The proviso to section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 names agreements and action under them, not codes, and states no time limit; the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the section 5 exemption for past action under codes, and whatever exemption survives for past action is an accrued effect, not continued operation of this approval. Nothing in the held sources continues the approval after June 14, 1935.

A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U.S. 495, decided May 27, 1935: the Court held the section 3 code-making delegation unconstitutional and the Live Poultry Code provisions in question invalid. Recorded as a validity characterization for every section 3 code approval, not as this order's end; the judgment did not cancel or withdraw this order.

NIRA section 3 (48 Stat. 195, June 16, 1933): under 3(a) the President approved codes and could impose conditions of approval; under 3(b), 3(c) and 3(f) an approved code's provisions became standards of fair competition enforceable by injunction and as misdemeanors. These are the legal effects that section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed.

NIRA section 5 exempted from the antitrust laws any code approved and in effect under Title I and any complying action while Title I was in effect and for sixty days thereafter; any exemption for action taken before the repeal is an accrued effect, not continued operation of the approval.

Acts done under the approved code before June 14, 1935, and any liability for violating it before that date, are accrued effects. The general savings statute of the time (not a held source) preserved liabilities already incurred under a repealed statute; that preservation does not keep the approval operative. Section 5 of the Act exempted from the antitrust laws "any code, agreement, or license approved, prescribed, or issued and in effect under this title" and complying action while Title I was in effect and for sixty days after; whatever exemption survives for action taken before the repeal is an accrued effect. The proviso in section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 says the exemption "shall extend only to agreements and action thereunder" of two kinds (section 7(a) requirements, and prohibiting practices already unlawful); it names agreements, not codes, and states no time limit, so the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the exemption for action taken under codes before June 14, 1935. I read the complete held Federal Register original of Executive Order 7577 (2 FR 671, March 24, 1937; signed March 19, 1937). It is one order that amends section XV-4 of the Instructions to Diplomatic Officers and section 451 of the Consular Regulations to read as a new text on presents and testimonials, and that text prohibits diplomatic and consular officers from accepting any present, decoration, medal, order or testimonial from a foreign king, prince or state. It has no duration, condition, report or savings language. I read the complete held Federal Register text of Executive Order 8396 (5 FR 1461, April 20, 1940; signed April 18, 1940). Under its heading revoking executive orders, it states that the listed executive orders are revoked, and the list includes Executive Order No. 7577 dated March 19, 1937, with no condition, exception or deferred effective date. That express revocation is the first end of the order. I read the coverage notes of the three machine searches before selecting them: the U.S. Code search (edition through 2026-10-09, so laws enacted in the last five days before the 2026-10-14 cutoff are not reflected) and the eCFR search (as of 2026-10-14) found no citation of this order, and the Federal Register disposition-note search found the revocation by Executive Order 8396 and a catalog note that is blank about its effect, which the held revocation text supplies. No held instrument restores or revives Executive Order 7577 after the revocation. Original not an original grade issue: the Federal Register text layer is machine extracted and was checked only as text; the page images were not inspected.

Executive Order 7636 (official Federal Register text, 2 FR 1259, PDF pages 1-1, read in the saved OCR text layer of the govinfo issue PDF: heading, enacting clause, operative text and signature/filing line are all present) permits state, county or municipal officers elected by grazing-district voters and appointed by the Secretary of the Interior to serve as district advisors under the Taylor Grazing Act of June 28, 1934. Its whole operative content is an amendment of Executive Order No. 9 of January 17, 1873, as amended (the 1989 OFR disposition table: 'Amended EO 9'; 'Revoked by EO 11408'). EO 11408 of April 25, 1968 (33 FR 6459, saved official text read in full) revoked EO 9 itself in section 1 and in section 2 revoked 'All prior Executive orders insofar as they interpret or amend Executive Order No. 9'; EO 11408 section 2 names it expressly in its list of revoked amendatory orders. Because the order consists only of that amendment, 'insofar as' reaches all of it, which is also why the OFR catalog's '(in part)' qualifier on some of these notes does not leave any part in force. EO 11408 states no effective date, so the revocation took effect on signing, 1968-04-25. No earlier end was found: the order has no expiry, condition or temporary term, the OFR catalog and the saved-text corpus show no earlier amendment or revocation, and the U.S. Code and eCFR searches show no current citation. Each clause therefore first ended on 1968-04-25 and that is the whole-order end. OCR quotations keep the scan's recognition errors (and soft hyphens) exactly as held; they have not been compared with page images.

EO 11408 contains no savings, transition or continuation clause. Its section 1 revoked Executive Order No. 9 of January 17, 1873 (the dual federal-state office-holding prohibition) itself, and section 2 revoked every prior order insofar as it interpreted or amended that order. This order's only operative content is an amendment of (an exception to) that 1873 order, so once the prohibition itself was revoked nothing remained for the exception to operate on, and no office, fund, property, entitlement or enforceable right was created by the order that could survive; office-holding done under the permission before 1968 was lawful when done and is a completed historical fact, not a continuing effect.

EO 11408 contains no savings, transition or continuation clause. Its section 1 revoked Executive Order No. 9 of January 17, 1873 (the dual federal-state office-holding prohibition) itself, and section 2 revoked every prior order insofar as it interpreted or amended that order. This order's only operative content is an amendment of (an exception to) that 1873 order, so once the prohibition itself was revoked nothing remained for the exception to operate on, and no office, fund, property, entitlement or enforceable right was created by the order that could survive; office-holding done under the permission before 1968 was lawful when done and is a completed historical fact, not a continuing effect.

EO 7921 (June 30, 1938) extended the existence of the Quetico-Superior Committee for four years, from June 30, 1938 to June 30, 1942. The Quetico-Superior Committee was created by EO 6783 (1934) for a limited period and kept alive by successive four-year extension orders (EOs 7921, 9213, 9741, 10134, 10541, 10767, 11031) and amended by EOs 9890, 10589 and 11031. EO 11342 of April 10, 1967 (32 FR 5827) established a committee of the same name anew (sec. 1), let it carry forward the old committee's uncompleted business (sec. 5) and in sec. 6 superseded EO 6783 and all nine continuing or amending orders; it states no effective date, so it took effect on signing. That supersession was a formal cleanup: each extension order had already run out on the fixed date it states, and the last extension (EO 11031 sec. 1) ended on June 30, 1966. The 1989 Codification disposition row for EO 6783 lists no continuation after EO 11031, the OFR catalog has no Quetico order between EO 11031 and EO 11342, and EO 11342 establishes the committee anew, so the committee lapsed on June 30, 1966. The 1989 Codification ('Superseded by EO 11342') and the OFR catalog note were used only as leads; the dates come from the order texts. Texts were checked against the text layer of the saved official Federal Register scans (fr-originals); no page-image comparison was made. This order's only operative provision is the extension itself, so its operation ended on 1942-06-30; the 1967 supersession is recorded as a later event.

Neither this order nor EO 11342 contains a savings clause preserving any provision of this order. EO 11342 sec. 5 lets the new committee carry forward uncompleted business and succeed to records and property of the committee provided for in EO 6783; that is a successor-order transition for the committee's affairs, not a continuation of this order's terms.

Its whole operative content is an amendment of Executive Order No. 9 of January 17, 1873, as amended (the 1989 OFR disposition table: 'Amended EO 9'; 'Revoked by EO 11408'). EO 11408 of April 25, 1968 (33 FR 6459, saved official text read in full) revoked EO 9 itself in section 1 and in section 2 revoked 'All prior Executive orders insofar as they interpret or amend Executive Order No. 9'; EO 11408 section 2 names it expressly in its list of revoked amendatory orders. Because the order consists only of that amendment, 'insofar as' reaches all of it, which is also why the OFR catalog's '(in part)' qualifier on some of these notes does not leave any part in force. EO 11408 states no effective date, so the revocation took effect on signing, 1968-04-25. No earlier end was found: the order has no expiry, condition or temporary term, the OFR catalog and the saved-text corpus show no earlier amendment or revocation, and the U.S. Code and eCFR searches show no current citation. Each clause therefore first ended on 1968-04-25 and that is the whole-order end. OCR quotations keep the scan's recognition errors (and soft hyphens) exactly as held; they have not been compared with page images.

EO 11408 contains no savings, transition or continuation clause. Its section 1 revoked Executive Order No. 9 of January 17, 1873 (the dual federal-state office-holding prohibition) itself, and section 2 revoked every prior order insofar as it interpreted or amended that order. This order's only operative content is an amendment of (an exception to) that 1873 order, so once the prohibition itself was revoked nothing remained for the exception to operate on, and no office, fund, property, entitlement or enforceable right was created by the order that could survive; office-holding done under the permission before 1968 was lawful when done and is a completed historical fact, not a continuing effect.

EO 8546 (Sept. 24, 1940; 5 FR 3817-3818) creates the Defense Communications Board (para. 1), gives it planning functions for national emergencies (para. 2), sets its chairmanship and secretary (para. 3), its scope and broadcasting studies (para. 4), committees (paras. 5-6), consultation (para. 7), the advisory role of the Interdepartment Radio Advisory Committee during war or national emergency (para. 8) and reporting to the President (para. 9). Later events: EO 8960 (Dec. 6, 1941) substituted the Treasury officer named in paras. 1 and 3; EO 9183 (June 15, 1942) renamed the Board the Board of War Communications and amended this order accordingly; neither ended a clause (word substitutions; the clauses continue as amended). EO 8964 and EO 9089 gave the Board further powers without amending this order. The orders rest on wartime and emergency powers (Communications Act sec. 606 and the national emergency); neither the orders nor sec. 606 had lapsed before Feb. 24, 1947: the state of war declared in December 1941 had not been terminated, and no concurrent resolution ending the sec. 606 powers is recorded in the bounded sources; no earlier presidential order ending any of these provisions appears in the OFR catalog or the saved order texts. EO 9831 (Feb. 24, 1947; 12 FR 1363) para. 1 abolishes the Board, created 'as the Defense Communications Board by Executive Order No. 8546', and para. 2 revokes EO 8546; it states no effective date, so it took effect on issuance. Every clause therefore first ended on 1947-02-24, the whole-order end. The two current-law hits (47 U.S.C. 606 note) print EO 9831 itself, which confirms the abolition and revocation; no current predicate. The 1989 Codification row: 'Amended by EOs 8960, 9183 ... Revoked by EO 9831'.

EO 9831 para. 1 abolishes the Board of War Communications and transfers all its property and records to the Federal Communications Commission; para. 2 revokes the five orders without any savings clause. The Board's records and property pass to the FCC; claims to just compensation for any government use or control of facilities rest on Communications Act sec. 606 itself, not on the revoked orders. No continuing effect rests on this order.

EO 8674 (Feb. 6, 1941; 6 FR 831) has one operative provision: it further amends EO 7293 so that enlisted men on duty at the naval attaché office at Havana, Cuba, not furnished quarters or rations in kind, receive a per diem of $3.00 in lieu of subsistence and $1.00 in lieu of quarters. No order changed that provision before EO 8704 (Mar. 4, 1941), which prescribes a complete new set of allowance regulations and 'shall supersede Executive Order No. 7293 ... as amended by' EOs 7831, 8107, 8440 and 8674, 'effec­tive as of the date hereof except as to quarters allowance within the continental limits of the United States' (July 1, 1941). This provision concerns duty abroad, so it was superseded on March 4, 1941, the first end and whole-order end. The OFR catalog note ('Superseded by: EO 8704, March 4, 1941') and the 1989 Codification ('Superseded by EO 8704') agree. The operative words quoted in original_operative_text are complete for the amendment; the opening words of the sentence (EO 8674) or its continuation after the issue's contents column (EO 8440) are quoted in original_source, and the OCR's footnote-marked citations of the earlier amending orders (printed '78311', '81078', '84408') are left out of the quotations. No human certification is asserted.

EO 8704 contains no savings clause; it restates the whole allowance table itself (Table I, Exception No. 4 covers the embassies and legations concerned at its own rates). Allowances already paid under the superseded order are completed payments, not continuing effects. Bounded search: this order and EO 8704 in full.

EO 8744 (April 24, 1941; 6 FR 2118-2119, held official FR scan text, closing tag '[No. 8744]') has a single operative paragraph: an incumbent of a position covered into the classified service by section 1 of EO 8743 who is involuntarily separated by reduction in force, abolition of the position or liquidation of the agency between the date of EO 8743 and the effective date of its section 1 may acquire a classified status for transfer, provided (among other things) that 'he obtains such transfer within one year from the date of his separation'. By its own terms the authorization could therefore operate only for separations up to the effective date of section 1 of EO 8743 (January 1, 1942 under EO 8743 Sec. 2, earlier for positions that fell vacant after June 30, 1941) and transfers within one year after them. The EO 12608 revocation of September 9, 1987 is a formal cleanup that follows this earlier cessation and is recorded as a later event, not the first end. The exact last day cannot yet be fixed: EO 8743 Sec. 2 was itself amended (EOs 9230, 9358, 9678, 9712 and others touch EO 8743) and it is not established whether any amendment moved the effective date of its section 1; and a transfer deadline is a condition of eligibility, so the date must be fixed from the text, not inferred.

EO 12608 Sec. 1 provides that notwithstanding the revocation of EO 8744, benefits already conferred under it before revocation shall not be affected: classified status acquired under the order stands.

Content: the order has one recital and one operative sentence. It further exempts one named employee, Harry T. Edwards (senior technologist, Bureau of Plant Industry, Department of Agriculture), from compulsory retirement for age under section 204 of the act of June 30, 1932, 47 Stat. 382, 404 (U.S.C., title 5, sec. 715a), for a period of one year ending October 31, 1941. The recital says he "was exempted from compulsory retirement for age for periods totaling two years by Executive Orders No. 8259 of September 21, 1939, and No. 8525 of August 26, 1940" and asks that he "be further exempted from such compulsory retirement for a period of one year"; those earlier orders (EO 8259 and EO 8525) are earlier instruments, not later events and not ends of this order. Edwards" and provides that this order is amended; the held sentence reads "is hereby amended so as to exempt Mr. Edwards from compulsory retirement for a period of one year ending October 31, 1942". EO 8844 was signed on 1941-08-08, before the original last day (October 31, 1941), so the clause was still running when its period was changed. Under the owner ruling of 2026-10-21 on strike-and-insert amendments, the clause continues, amended, and the amendment is a later event that records the clause text before and after: before, "a period of one year ending October 31, 1941"; after, "a period of one year ending October 31, 1942". The amendment changes the last day by one year, so the substance of the period changed. The first end is therefore the amended last day, October 31, 1942, not the original October 31, 1941. EO 8844 states no separate effective date, so the amendment is recorded as effective on its date of signing, 1941-08-08.

Executive Order 8880 (official Federal Register text, 6 FR 4551, PDF pages 1-1, read in the saved OCR text layer of the govinfo issue PDF: heading, enacting clause, operative text and signature/filing line are all present) permits a federal officer or employee to hold the office of Chancellor of the University of Puerto Rico, with a non-interference proviso. Its whole operative content is an amendment of Executive Order No. 9 of January 17, 1873, as amended (the 1989 OFR disposition table: 'Amended EO 9'; 'Revoked by EO 11408'). EO 11408 of April 25, 1968 (33 FR 6459, saved official text read in full) revoked EO 9 itself in section 1 and in section 2 revoked 'All prior Executive orders insofar as they interpret or amend Executive Order No. 9'; EO 11408 section 2 names it expressly in its list of revoked amendatory orders. Because the order consists only of that amendment, 'insofar as' reaches all of it, which is also why the OFR catalog's '(in part)' qualifier on some of these notes does not leave any part in force. EO 11408 states no effective date, so the revocation took effect on signing, 1968-04-25. No earlier end was found: the order has no expiry, condition or temporary term, the OFR catalog and the saved-text corpus show no earlier amendment or revocation, and the U.S. Code and eCFR searches show no current citation. Each clause therefore first ended on 1968-04-25 and that is the whole-order end. OCR quotations keep the scan's recognition errors (and soft hyphens) exactly as held; they have not been compared with page images.

EO 11408 contains no savings, transition or continuation clause. Its section 1 revoked Executive Order No. 9 of January 17, 1873 (the dual federal-state office-holding prohibition) itself, and section 2 revoked every prior order insofar as it interpreted or amended that order. This order's only operative content is an amendment of (an exception to) that 1873 order, so once the prohibition itself was revoked nothing remained for the exception to operate on, and no office, fund, property, entitlement or enforceable right was created by the order that could survive; office-holding done under the permission before 1968 was lawful when done and is a completed historical fact, not a continuing effect.

Identity: the register lists this number with date 1941-09-22, signer Franklin D. Roosevelt and the title "Exemption of Maurice C. Clauses are quoted from that registered file, not from the unregistered clause-drafts copy.
Content: the order has one recital and one operative sentence. It exempts one named employee, Maurice C. Latta (Executive Clerk, The White House Office, Executive Office of the President), from compulsory retirement for age under section 204 of the act of June 30, 1932, 47 Stat. 382, 404 (U.S.C., title 5, sec. 715a), for a period of one year ending October 31, 1942. The recital says he "was exempted from compulsory retirement for age for periods totaling two years by Executive Orders No. 8256 of September 20, 1939, and No. 8497 of July 26, 1940" and asks that he "be further exempted from such compulsory retirement for a period of one year"; the earlier exemption orders it recites are earlier instruments, not later events, and not ends of this order. The inventory is therefore one clause, the exemption. Extension reading: this order is the further exemption; any later exemption of the same person would be a new exercise of the section 204 power with its own period and a later event, not an end of this order, and EO 9238 is such an order (below).
Later event: EO 9238 of September 3, 1942 (APP node 371719; page check done 2026-11-04 in jobs/app-executive-orders/output/MIRROR_DOCUMENTS.jsonl: heading "Executive Order 9238—Exemption of Rudolph Forster and Maurice C. Latta from Compulsory Retirement for Age", date 1942-09-03, text_sha256 equal to the held file's, Common Crawl capture 2025-06-12T16:58:17Z) exempts Rudolph Forster and further exempts Maurice C. Latta, Executive Clerk, The White House Office. Its recital says Latta "who has heretofore been exempted from compulsory retirement for age until October 31, 1942", which is the same position and the same last day as this order; its operative sentence ("are hereby exempted and further exempted, respectively, from compulsory retirement for age" "the said Rudolph Forster and Maurice C. Latte", which spells his surname "Latte") states no period. It does not revoke, supersede or amend this order and it recites this order's exemption as a completed grant, so it is a further exemption recorded as a later event with its own date and quote (owner ruling 2026-10-21 on further exemptions), not this order's end. The period it grants after October 31, 1942 is not this order's command.

The orders rest on wartime and emergency powers (Communications Act sec. 606 and the national emergency); neither the orders nor sec. 606 had lapsed before Feb. 24, 1947: the state of war declared in December 1941 had not been terminated, and no concurrent resolution ending the sec. 606 powers is recorded in the bounded sources; no earlier presidential order ending any of these provisions appears in the OFR catalog or the saved order texts. EO 9831 para. 1 abolishes the Board of War Communications and transfers all its property and records to the Federal Communications Commission; para. 2 revokes the five orders without any savings clause. No continuing effect rests on this order.
